title:
Challenges in the Diagnosis and Treatment of Neuromyelitis Optica
Spectrum Disorders: A Case Report With a Brief Review of
Literature
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man of Asian Indian descent with no prior neurologic disease presented on day 1 with frontal and binocular ocular pain and a rapid decline in visual acuity. He had normal brain CT and retinal fluorescein angiography. Routine blood tests, renal and hepatic panels, fasting glucose, complete blood count, inflammatory markers, serum proteins, iron studies, vitamin B12, folate, urinalysis, and toxicology (blood lead, trichloroethanol; urine methanol, trichloroacetic acid, lead) were all within normal limits or undetectable. Tests for systemic infection were negative. Visual-evoked potentials showed delayed P100 latency bilaterally. He was diagnosed with bilateral optic neuritis and received IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days without improvement in vision.

On day 5, he developed rapidly worsening paraparesis with bladder dysfunction. Brain and total spinal cord MRI revealed an 8 mm T2-hyperintense, noncontrast-enhancing lesion in the left parietal subcortical white matter, additional small nonspecific T2-hyperintense subcortical lesions, and three thoracic spinal cord lesions (<3 vertebral segments) that were T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense, and contrast-enhancing.

On day 20, neurologic examination showed paraparetic gait (right > left), lower-limb weakness with mild right spasticity, hyperreflexia with right ankle clonus, bilateral Babinski signs, and visual acuity reduced to hand motion in both eyes. Cognition and upper-limb function were intact. CSF analysis revealed protein 71 mg/dL, 4 cells/mm^3, and absence of oligoclonal bands. CNS infectious workup was negative. Serum screening for autoimmune diseases (ANA, ENA panel, ANCA, AMA, ASMA, APCA, anticardiolipin, anti-TPO, anti-TG, ACE) was negative, and serum neoplastic markers were normal. Both serum myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG and aquaporin-4 IgG, tested by cell-based assays and repeated in a second laboratory, were negative. A second course of IV methylprednisolone was administered, yielding partial improvement in paraparesis but no change in visual deficit.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious etiology was considered — “Signs of an existing systemic infectious disease were absent (Table 1).”  
2. Other autoimmune/inflammatory disorders (ADEM, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren syndrome, neuro-Behçet disease, sarcoidosis, primary angiitis of the CNS, paraneoplastic and autoimmune encephalitis) were excluded — “because of the absence of typical clinical, humoral, and radiological (MRI, chest X-ray) findings (Table 2).”  
3. Multiple sclerosis was deemed unlikely — “because of the absence of most MS-typical clinical and radiological features apart from short myelitis (eg, monolateral and mild-to-moderate ON, … type 2 OBs).”  
4. Neuromyelitis optica under 2006 criteria could not be diagnosed — “because of the lack of serum AQP4-IgG and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM).”  
5. NMOSD by 2015 AQP4-IgG–negative criteria was not satisfied — “because the required association between acute myelitis and LETM was not fulfilled.”  
6. MOG-IgG–associated disorder was excluded — “In our case, the former has been excluded, while the latter has not been tested.”
